Sierra History · The Road Over Carson Pass

The Mormon Emigrant Trail

In the summer of 1848, forty-five discharged soldiers of the Mormon Battalion — and one eighteen-year-old bride — turned their backs on the richest gold discovery in American history and spent forty days building a wagon road over the Sierra. Then the whole Gold Rush came pouring up it the other way.

Every road over the Sierra had to be built twice: once by the people who first forced wagons across it, and once by everyone who followed. The road over Carson Pass — the road Highway 88 still roughly follows, the road that runs past Silver Lake and Caples Lake an hour from Fiddletown — was built the first time by men walking away from California.

They were veterans of the Mormon Battalion, discharged soldiers who had spent the winter of 1847–48 working for John Sutter — some of them at the very sawmill where gold was found that January. They knew exactly what they were leaving. They had families waiting a thousand miles east, in a new city on the shore of the Great Salt Lake, and no wagon road home. The known route, up the Truckee River past Donner Lake, meant crossing the river again and again and climbing a pass that had eaten the Donner Party two winters before. So they decided to make a road of their own, south of the lake, over the pass Kit Carson had crossed on snowshoes in 1844 — following, as they knew, a much older Washoe trail over the crest.

It took them about forty days. It cost three of them their lives before they were halfway. And within a year, the road they built to leave California had become one of the main doors into it.

Chapter One

The battalion comes to California

The Mormon Battalion was a strange unit: the only one in American military history recruited entirely from a single religious group. In July 1846, with the Latter-day Saints driven out of Illinois and camped in refugee settlements along the Missouri River, the U.S. Army mustered more than five hundred Mormon volunteers for the war with Mexico. Their families stayed behind in the camps. The men marched west under orders to open a wagon road to California.

And march they did — some 2,000 miles, among the longest infantry marches in American history: down the Rio Grande, across the deserts of what is now Arizona, fighting one comic-opera battle against a herd of wild bulls on the San Pedro River, and cutting Cooke's Wagon Road across the Southwest as they went. They reached San Diego on January 29, 1847 — after the fighting in California had already ended. The battalion had been hired, in effect, as road builders with muskets, and road building was what it was good at.

Discharged at Los Angeles on July 16, 1847, the veterans scattered. Some reenlisted. Many headed north to find work and wait out the winter before attempting the journey east to their families, who by then were gathering in the Salt Lake Valley. Roughly a hundred of them ended up in the Sacramento area working for John Augustus Sutter — building his fort town, farming, and, for one small crew up the South Fork of the American River at Coloma, helping a carpenter named James Marshall build a sawmill.

That winter's work would put these men at the hinge of California history — twice. First at the sawmill. Then on the mountain.

Chapter Two

“Some kind of mettle”

On the morning of January 24, 1848, James Marshall picked flakes of gold out of the tailrace of Sutter's sawmill at Coloma. We know the exact date — for a fact that launched a world-changing rush, unusually, we do — because a battalion veteran working on the mill kept a diary. Henry William Bigler, 32 years old, wrote it down that night, spelling and all:

“Monday 24th — this day some kind of mettle was discover was found in the tail race that that looks like goald, first discovered by James Martial, the boss of the Mill.” Henry W. Bigler's diary, January 24, 1848

Marshall kept no diary and later misremembered the date; Bigler's plain entry, backed by fellow veteran Azariah Smith's journal, is the record history settled on. The men at the mill — Bigler, Smith, James S. Brown and others — were among the first people on earth to know California had gold in its rivers.

Which makes what they did next the most quietly astonishing part of this whole story. On April 9, 1848, the veterans working around Sutter's Fort settled their accounts. Sutter, cash-poor as always, paid them mostly in the things a journey needs: horses, mules, wagons, cattle, supplies. They took their pay in livestock, walked away from the gold country with the secret of the century in their pockets, and started organizing to go home. Returning battalion members would eventually carry some $17,000 in gold east into the struggling Salt Lake economy — but gold was never the cargo that mattered most to them. Their families were.

In mid-June, Bigler and two companions rode out and picked a rendezvous: Pleasant Valley, in the foothills east of Placerville — a place that still carries the name they gave it. From June 21 the company gathered there: about forty-five men, seventeen wagons, two small cannons, roughly 150 horses and mules and as many cattle. And one woman — Melissa Burton Coray, eighteen years old, the bride of Sergeant William Coray, who had marched with the battalion as a laundress and simply never stopped marching. She was traveling pregnant, on her second battalion road-building expedition; she had watched these men cut Cooke's Wagon Road across the desert Southwest, and now she would watch them cut another one across the Sierra.

Why a new road?

The established California Trail crossed the Sierra far to the north, by Donner Pass, and its Truckee River canyon forced wagon after wagon through the same river dozens of times. The battalion men had heard of an Indigenous trail — a Washoe crossing — about twenty-five miles south of Donner Pass, over the crest near where Frémont and Carson had crossed in 1844. If they could thread wagons along the high divide between the American River and the streams to the south, they'd have a shorter, drier road — and a road of their own.

Chapter Three

Building the road

On July 3, 1848, the company rolled out of Pleasant Valley and turned its wagons up into the mountains — the first wagons ever to attempt this line, going the “wrong” way, west to east, out of California. History remembers them as the Holmes–Thompson company, after Jonathan Holmes and Samuel Thompson, the men who led it once the journey was underway. Their elected captain at the start was Daniel Browett — a fact that matters, painfully, a chapter from now.

There was no road. There was a direction: the long forested divide between the South Fork of the American River on the north and the Cosumnes River country on the south, climbing steadily from about 3,000 feet toward 9,000. A road crew worked ahead of the wagons, felling trees, rolling boulders, prying out stumps, and grading a bench wide enough for a wagon bed wherever the ridge narrowed to a knife edge. The wagons behind them were, in effect, testing the road by surviving it.

The pace tells the story of the work. It took the company fifteen days to blaze the first thirty-nine miles — barely two and a half miles a day. They named the landmarks as they went, the way road builders do: camps at Leek Spring, named for the wild leeks that grew around it; long dry stretches where every drop of water for men and stock had to be planned. Even in July, as they neared the crest, the journals record working through snow in places fifteen feet deep — the Sierra's winter still sitting on the high country, months after the lowland summer had begun.

If you drive the paved forest road between Sly Park and Highway 88 today — the one the maps label Mormon Emigrant Trail, long known locally as Iron Mountain Road — you are driving the descendant of this climb. The modern road wanders a little from the 1848 line, as roads do, but it holds the same divide, past the same springs, for the same reason: it's the route the battalion picked.

Ahead of the wagons, though, three men were missing — and had been missing for days.

Chapter Four

Tragedy Spring

Back at Pleasant Valley, Captain Daniel Browett had made the decision every trail captain makes: somebody had to scout ahead. On June 25, before the company even rolled, Browett rode out with two companions — Ezrah H. Allen and Henderson Cox — to reconnoiter the route over the mountains and report back. They were good men to send. Allen, a battalion veteran, carried his savings in a double gold pouch worn around his neck.

They never reported back. The company waited, then moved out anyway on July 3, expecting the scouts to reappear down the trail. A ten-man search party pushed ahead and came back on July 14 with nothing. Then, on July 18, the road crew working ahead of the wagons came to a spring in the high forest and found a cold campfire, broken and bloody arrows, blood-stained rocks — and a fresh, shallow grave.

On July 19 the main party reached the spring and opened the grave. Inside lay Browett, Allen, and Cox, stripped naked and crowded into the earth together; Browett had been struck in the face with an axe or hatchet. The company concluded the three had been murdered in their sleep on the night of June 27. In the brush nearby they found Allen's gold pouch, still holding some $100 in gold — apparently torn loose and lost in the dark during the attack. They carried it east, and in time it was delivered to Allen's widow, Sarah; it helped her and her two children make the journey to Utah.

The company laid over a day to do the thing properly. They dug a deeper grave, built a wall of rock around it some three feet high, and Wilford Hudson carved the names into a nearby fir: “To the Memory of Daniel Browett, Ezrah H. Allen, Henderson Cox, Who was supposed to have Been Murdered and Buried by Indians On the Night of the 27th June 1848.” Then they named the place for what had happened there — Tragedy Spring — and went back to building their road.

An honest note on the killers

The company blamed Native attackers, based on the arrows at the scene and reports of men seen wearing some of the scouts' clothing. That attribution has never been proven, and it has been questioned for a long time: Washoe descendants have pointed out that their people did not bury their dead, and would not have taken a dead man's property — yet the three were buried, and the gold pouch was left behind. The modern landmark plaque at the spring says the three were “murdered by unknown persons,” and unknown is where the record honestly leaves it.

The road they built, stop by stop

The company's July 1848 line over the Sierra — the route that became the Carson River Route of the California Trail. Tap each stop to walk it with them.

July 3, 1848 · The rendezvous

Pleasant Valley

The company rolls out: about 45 men, one woman, 17 wagons, 2 cannons, and some 300 head of horses, mules, and cattle. Henry Bigler had picked this gathering place on June 17. Ahead of them: no road at all — just a divide ridge climbing toward the crest, and three scouts already nine days overdue.

Chapter Five

Over the top

The road's crux came on July 24. Above Tragedy Spring the ridge rears up to West Pass, 9,550 feet — higher than Carson Pass itself, and, by the usual reckoning, the highest point ever crossed by an emigrant wagon road in the continental United States. The journals are blunt about the day: the grade was so rough and steep that one wagon tipped over twice, and many others broke down. These were not trail-wise emigrant wagons anymore; they were battered army-surplus freight, hauled up a mountainside by men who had been swinging axes for three weeks. They got every one of them over.

Two days of repairs, then down to the lake they called Lake Valley — today's Caples Lake — and on July 28 east through Carson Pass, where a pine still bore the name Kit Carson had carved into it on Valentine's Day 1844, four winters before. Frémont's party had crossed here desperate, on foot, eating their mules. The battalion company crossed with wagons, cattle, and two cannons, and left a road behind them.

The east side nearly undid the compliment. From the summit the road plunges down a pitch so steep that the company had to ease the wagons down to Red Lake, where they camped on Saturday night, July 29. Westbound travelers would meet that pitch head-on, and their name for it — Devil's Ladder — turns up in emigrant journal after emigrant journal for a decade: wagons unloaded, loads carried up on men's backs, teams doubled and redoubled, block and tackle rigged to trees to haul empty wagons up a slope some swore was steeper than a house roof.

On Sunday, July 30, they traveled five miles down the widening canyon and came out into a broad, grassy, well-watered valley — the first kind country in weeks. Their journals say they named it because it was the first real sign of hope that they would get out of the mountains. Hope Valley, it remains. Five more days down the canyon of the Carson River brought them out, on August 5, into Carson Valley itself. The road was done: roughly 170 miles of new wagon road in about forty days, over the highest wagon pass in America. The company turned north, joined the established California Trail, and followed the Humboldt River east. Its advance party rode into the Salt Lake Valley on September 28, 1848 — the Corays among those who arrived that fall, Melissa having now watched a road get built across half a continent, twice.

Melissa's peak

For 146 years the only woman on the journey had no monument but the journals. In 1994 that changed: the U.S. Board on Geographic Names officially named the 9,763-foot peak just south of West Pass Melissa Coray Peak, and on July 30 of that year the Oregon-California Trails Association dedicated the trail marker above Silver Lake pictured at the top of this story. The plaque's tribute is to “the heroic pioneering efforts of Melissa and similar women who endured hardships in settling the West.”

Chapter Six

The road reverses

The company had built the road to leave. The world used it to arrive. Word of the new crossing traveled east along the Humboldt with the company's own wagons, and beginning in August 1848 — within weeks of its completion — westbound emigrants were already following the battalion's tracks up the Carson River and over the pass. Then came the news from Coloma, and the trickle became the Gold Rush.

The Carson River Route, as the forty-niners knew it, became one of the great highways of the migration. Some 500 to 700 emigrants used it in its first season; over the next three years, estimates run from 20,000 to 50,000 people a year over Carson Pass, and one trail history reckons that in the few years after 1848 the road carried more than 50,000 wagons and 200,000 gold seekers in all. A surviving trail register gives the flavor of the traffic even in the summer of 1854, five years on: 800 wagons, 30,015 head of cattle, 1,903 horses and mules, and 8,550 sheep — counted past a single checkpoint, in a single season, on the road forty-six people had hacked out of the forest in 1848.

The westbound journals are a chorus of awe and profanity, most of it aimed at the Devil's Ladder. But the route had real virtues that kept it busy: it delivered emigrants directly into the southern Mother Lode — Placerville, then the Amador County diggings — and it avoided the Truckee's endless river crossings. Trading posts and stations grew up along it on both slopes; Woodfords, at the eastern foot of the canyon, began as a stop on this road. A decade later, when the Comstock silver strike reversed the flow again and fortune hunters poured east out of California, developers improved the old trail into the Amador–Carson Valley Wagon Road. For five weeks in 1860 the Pony Express rode a section of it. And through the late 1850s and beyond, a lone Norwegian on ten-foot skis carried the winter mail over these same passes, following the road the battalion had opened — Snowshoe Thompson, whose story is told elsewhere in this collection.

The railroad over Donner Pass in 1869 finally demoted the Carson road from highway to byway. But it never quite closed. It became a stock driveway, then a county road, then a state highway — the line on the land that Highway 88 still follows, from Carson Valley up the canyon, past Red Lake and Caples Lake, over the pass, and down the long divide past Tragedy Spring to Placerville and the foothills.

Epilogue

The trail today

You can still travel nearly all of this story in a single day's drive from Fiddletown, and most of it without leaving pavement. Highway 88 climbs the Carson River canyon from Woodfords exactly as the wagons did, passes Hope Valley's meadows, Red Lake, and the Devil's Ladder pitch (the highway switchbacks above it), crosses Carson Pass at 8,574 feet, and runs down past Caples Lake and Silver Lake along the northern edge of the old road's high country.

The western climb survives as its own road: the Mormon Emigrant Trail — Forest Road 10N50, long called Iron Mountain Road — a paved, roughly 24-mile drive through Eldorado National Forest from Sly Park Road to Highway 88 near Silver Lake. It follows the battalion's divide for much of its length, past the Old 49er Tree, whose trunk once carried a blaze reading “old 49 road” with an arrow for the emigrants who followed. The Forest Service closes it under winter snow, and Caltrans occasionally presses it into service as an emergency alternate to U.S. 50 — a 175-year-old road still doing detour duty.

At Tragedy Spring, a short turnoff west of Silver Lake, the story turns somber again. The site — grave cairn, plaques, picnic ground under the pines — was burned over by the Caldor Fire in August 2021, which scorched the whole corridor; the stone cairn over the three scouts survived, as it has through several rebuildings since 1848, and volunteers from the California Pioneer Heritage Foundation and Latter-day Saint congregations have been restoring the grounds since. The section of Hudson's carved fir, cut out and saved when the tree decayed, is kept indoors at the museum at Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park in Coloma — a few hundred yards from the millrace where Henry Bigler, who may well have known the carver, wrote the most famous misspelled sentence in California history.

Stand at the Carson Pass summit on a still morning and the whole arc of it is in view: a Washoe trail, a scout's snowshoe crossing, a battalion's wagon road, a gold rush highway, a ski-mail route, and a state highway, all threaded through the same notch in the granite. Roads are usually named for where they go. This one is named for who built it — forty-five soldiers and one young wife, going home.

The Journey & the Road

Their years, in brief

  • Jul 1846

    The battalion musters. More than 500 Mormon volunteers enlist in Iowa for the war with Mexico; their families remain in refugee camps on the Missouri.

  • Jan 29, 1847

    San Diego. After a 2,000-mile march spent largely building Cooke's Wagon Road, the battalion reaches the Pacific — after the fighting in California has ended.

  • Jul 16, 1847

    Discharge. The battalion is mustered out at Los Angeles. Many veterans head north to work for John Sutter and wait out the winter.

  • Jan 24, 1848

    “Some kind of mettle.” James Marshall finds gold at Sutter's Mill, Coloma. Battalion veteran Henry Bigler records the date in his diary — the entry history relies on.

  • Apr 9, 1848

    Settling accounts. The veterans settle with Sutter, taking much of their pay in horses, wagons, and livestock — and turn their backs on the gold fields.

  • Jun 25, 1848

    The scouts ride out. Captain Daniel Browett, Ezrah H. Allen, and Henderson Cox leave Pleasant Valley to reconnoiter the route. They are killed, the company believes, on the night of June 27.

  • Jul 3, 1848

    Departure. About 45 men, Melissa Coray, 17 wagons, 2 cannons, and some 300 head of stock roll out of Pleasant Valley to build the road east.

  • Jul 19, 1848

    Tragedy Spring. The company finds and reburies its three scouts, walls the grave with rock, carves their names into a fir, and names the spring.

  • Jul 24, 1848

    West Pass. Wagons tip and break, but all cross at 9,550 feet — the highest wagon crossing on the emigrant trails.

  • Jul 28–30, 1848

    Carson Pass to Hope Valley. The company crosses Carson Pass, descends to Red Lake past the future Devil's Ladder, and names Hope Valley for the hope it gives them.

  • Sep 28, 1848

    Salt Lake Valley. The advance party arrives home. The road behind them — 170 miles of it — is open.

  • 1849–54

    The road reverses. The Carson River Route becomes a principal Gold Rush highway: tens of thousands a year over the pass, 800 wagons and 30,015 cattle counted in the 1854 season alone.

  • 1860

    Pony Express. For five weeks the express rides a section of the old trail to Woodfords; Snowshoe Thompson is already skiing the route with the mail.

  • 1994

    Melissa's peak. The peak south of West Pass is named Melissa Coray Peak, and the Oregon-California Trails Association dedicates the trail marker above Silver Lake.

  • 2021

    Caldor Fire. The fire burns through Tragedy Spring and the Mormon Emigrant Trail corridor; the grave cairn survives, and restoration by volunteers follows.

Stand Where It Happened

Places you can visit

Tragedy Spring — Highway 88, west of Silver Lake

California Historical Landmark No. 315: the rock-walled grave of Browett, Allen, and Cox, memorial plaques, and a picnic area in the pines, a short drive off the highway. Burned in the 2021 Caldor Fire and under volunteer restoration — go gently.

Carson Pass Summit & the OCTA Marker

The 8,574-foot summit where the wagon road crossed, with the 1994 Mormon–Carson Pass Emigrant Trail plaque on its granite boulder above Silver Lake and Melissa Coray Peak on the southern skyline.

Caples Lake & the Emigrant Trail

The company's “Lake Valley” camp of July 26, 1848. A hiking trail along the lake's south shore follows surviving stretches of the historic emigrant road.

Hope Valley & Woodfords

The valley the company named on July 30, 1848, still a broad open meadow on Highway 88 — and Woodfords, the trading-post settlement at the canyon's foot that grew up serving the road's traffic.

Mormon Emigrant Trail (Iron Mountain Road)

The paved Forest Service road from Sly Park to Highway 88, following the battalion's divide route past the Old 49er Tree. Open seasonally — closed under winter snow, as the original was meant to be traveled in summer.

Marshall Gold Discovery SHP — Coloma

Sutter's Mill site, Bigler's Coloma, and the museum holding the carved section of the Tragedy Spring fir — the two halves of this story, gold and road, in one park.
